description: Test your knowledge of PA BS1 | Bone & Soft Tissue with a focus on osteomyelitis classification, pathogenesis, and morphology.

cards.text: What is the most common causative organism in osteomyelitis and what percentage of cases does it account for?
cards.answer: Staphylococcus aureus accounts for 80–90% of all osteomyelitis cases across all age groups and infection routes.

tip.tip: S. aureus = 80–90% — remember the "golden" staph causes "golden" bone infections

cards.text: Name the three routes of osteomyelitis infection and the typical setting for each.
cards.answer: Hematogenous (children, metaphysis via bacteremia), contiguous spread (adults post-trauma/surgery, diabetic foot), direct inoculation (any age, open fractures/surgery).

cards.text: Why does hematogenous osteomyelitis preferentially lodge in the bone metaphysis in children?
cards.answer: The metaphyseal sinusoids have slow blood flow, reduced phagocytic activity, and lack tight junctions, allowing bacteria to extravasate and seed easily — combined with the large vascular surface area, this creates a perfect nidus.

tip.tip: Slow flow + loose junctions + low immunity = metaphyseal trap

cards.text: Define a sequestrum and explain its clinical significance.
cards.answer: A sequestrum is a segment of dead, necrotic cortical bone that cannot be resorbed by osteoclasts (they require living bone). It acts as a permanent nidus of infection and perpetuates chronic osteomyelitis.

tip.tip: Sequestrum = SEQuester — trapped, dead bone that cannot be removed naturally

cards.text: What is an involucrum and what does its presence indicate?
cards.answer: An involucrum is new bone formed by the surviving periosteum around and outside an infected zone, creating a reactive shell. It indicates a chronic, walled-off infection that the body has attempted to contain.

tip.tip: Involucrum = Wrapping — periosteum wraps the infection with new bone

cards.text: Which organism classically causes osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease?
cards.answer: Salmonella typhi is the classic organism in sickle cell osteomyelitis (a high-yield viva question), though S. aureus remains common.

tip.tip: Sickle cell + Salmonella = Classic viva pairing (functional asplenia increases risk)

cards.text: What is the most serious complication of hematogenous osteomyelitis in infants less than 1 year old?
cards.answer: Septic arthritis — vessels crossing the epiphyseal plate allow pus to track into the joint space, causing joint infection and potential permanent damage.

tip.tip: Infant OM → joint seeding (vessels cross growth plate before fusion)

cards.text: Differentiate acute, subacute, and chronic osteomyelitis by typical duration and key feature.
cards.answer: Acute (<3 weeks): purulent inflammation, no bone loss yet. Subacute (3 weeks–3 months): begins to show bone necrosis. Chronic (>3 months): devitalized bone, sinus tracts, requires surgical debridement.

tip.tip: A-S-C: Acute (pus), Subacute (starting necrosis), Chronic (sinuses + surgery)
